prayer.text: Saints Marcellinus and Peter, pray for us.

cues.text: Marcellinus , a Roman priest, and Peter , who served the Church as an exorcist, were both members of the Roman clergy.
An exorcist was an official minor order responsible for praying over and assisting those afflicted by evil spirits.
They were arrested during the harsh escalation of Diocletian's persecution in 304, which specifically targeted the Church's ordained ministers.
Rather than fall silent in captivity, tradition holds that the two continued their pastoral work even in prison.

They strengthened fellow Christian captives' faith and reportedly converted their jailer, his wife, and daughter—a detail that, whatever its precise historical accuracy, reflects the Church's memory of these martyrs as men who kept preaching to the very end.

According to Pope St. Damasus I , who as a boy heard the story firsthand from the executioner who had carried out the killing and later became a Christian himself, the judge deliberately ordered Marcellinus and Peter executed secretly.
This occurred in a remote thicket some three miles outside Rome, so that other Christians would have no place to venerate their remains.
The two men, according to this account, were forced to clear the briars and dig their own graves before being beheaded on the spot.
The location of their hidden burial was not lost, however: tradition holds that a devout Roman woman was shown the site in a vision, allowing their remains to be properly recovered and enshrined.

Pope Damasus later composed a commemorative epitaph in their honor, praising them for having brought, in his words, 'many unbelievers to the knowledge of the true faith' even from within a Roman prison cell.

Marcellinus and Peter are named together in the ancient Roman Canon of the Mass, still used in celebrations that employ the Roman Canon, Eucharistic Prayer I. This places them permanently among the small number of early martyrs whose memory the Church built directly into its central act of worship.
Their joint feast preserves the memory of two clergymen who, even facing a deliberately anonymous execution, continued to make disciples until the very end of their lives.
